text: Honestly speaking, I'd say the lack of stock and scalpers are definitely a big problem now, but try to look at the long term. Once stock comes back, in store pricing will come down, and scalpers will have to sell them off for vastly lower prices than they're asking right now, probably making a loss on it. Combine the stock that'll be in stores with the large amount of cards that scalpers will still have by then, and that's one hell of a large supply. Pricing will go down even lower! So be smart, keep using your 1070 or 1060 for another year (those aren't exactly slow either!) and don't sell them for a marginally increased price. They're worth a bit more now than say last year, but long term the price drops from the current 20 and 30 series will be much bigger, I'm guessing.

text:
Jay, I'd like to see you touch on this:

Just because you open your new card and get ecstatic that it pulled crazy 10% overclocks in heaven or timespy, a lot of people might not know that it's not a real-world indicator most of the time.  

I would wager a large amount of cards that find their max potential where they are "stable", actually have a good chance of just being so for the 5,10,20 minute benchmark runs.  Cool for getting scores, but even early on they may still struggle with random instability an hour or three into a steamy session of gaming and ruin your experience (forgot to save, were online, etc).

Most often, this degradation takes months or years to occur.  Sometimes it happens only on certain games.  My 3+ years old card can get +120 and +500 on several titles, but relatively easy titles like world of tanks will crash after a couple of matches with even a +50 & + 100.

I am mostly concerned that many will watch videos like this and think that their card will not only do these numbers out of the box, but also do those numbers indefinitely.

Just food for thought!
author: @Nathan-ct9eh

text:
It really depends on the software (game). Some just don't like overclocks at all. 
On my 1060, if I apply any form of overclock while playing Warframe theres a high chance of crashing when loading.
Yet when running Blender I can apply +150 core, +600 mem just fine. (of course Blender will be mostly using the CUDA cores, not all of the cores)
Valheim seems to be stable with overclocking as well but I haven't pushed it as high due to temp issues. (Have done +50 core, +450 meme stable).

Yes wear and tear/degregation will effect performance over time. However its a case by case situation with most cards

text:
@JammyBriton  Agreed.  My main point is that alot of people may walk away with "oh wow any 3060 I get is going to get a 10% bump and its going to work in every game because it passed Jayz benchmark!"

text: Note that overclocking the RAM on 30 series doesn't always mean higher performance. It actually is ECC on the 30 series so at some point when it becomes really broken you start losing performance. You have to actively monitor if your scores go up or down when bringing the speed up.
author: @Skylancer727

text: what values do you use?
author: @arian4562

text: @arian4562  you kinda just have to keep checking the scores. Because it's ECC errors won't cause the GPU to crash, but as they become more common your overall score or average frame rate will drop. This is because ECC is mainly ment to stop crashing, each error takes time to correct so the more you get the longer the code takes to move on. So there's a sweet spot where your score will keep going up but after that your score will slowly tick back down. So let's say you get a card with a default memory speed of 18000hz. The sweet point may be around 19500-20500hz. Beyond that point your scores and frame rates will slowly get worse as more errors happen.

text: i wonder: can you really trust a sample gpu received directly from the manufacturer? What stops them from manipulating the card in some way that makes it perform much better than the regular cards will be available in future? author: @schwarzarbyter

text:
That has definitely happened in the past (there was a Kingston SSD that was different for reviews than what retail actually was) however to get the card to use a 3060ti core but appear as a 3060 with the perf of a 3060ti requires a modified bios, and nvidia drivers will not install without modification on such a card.

Nvidia also heavily lock down the bios to prevent it from being modified in the first place, but assuming that the aib does circumvent those restrictions, the manufacturer can't modify the bios in that way without it being detectable, nor can they do it without risking losing their access to future GPU cores, and nvidia can be extremely vindictive to aib's that don't toe the line.

These companies might send a cherry picked card, but usually it doesn't take long for the real expected overclocking results for the average card to be discovered.

I'm not saying it can never happen, but the aib's have more to lose by cheating than they will gain, and nvidia make it extremely difficult to begin with.

text:
Soon, no. It'll get better eventually, but it probably won't normalize until a number of the new fabs in the works come fully online. But there's many aspects at play here that very few talk about.

Covid situation improving will help, by somewhat normalizing the shipping situation. That seems vaguely understood by some, at least it has been mentioned once or twice the last year. 

But a big one few if anyone mention, is the (blank) silicon wafer shortage. This has been staring us in the face for a decade. Demand has ever increased, but as fab companies have made more and more money per wafer, new nodes placing ever more tight demands of wafer supply and quality - these companies have refused to pay anywhere near reasonable prices for wafers. The result of this is that the companies manufacturing the wafers, have barely been able to fund scaling up and keep running older type production, like 200mm wafers, with little to no ability to fund newer modern production and facilities. Demand made the need to move to 300mm wafers as standard, patently obvious 15+ years ago, and would ideally be made a reality 8-10 years ago. But the refusal by Samsung, TSMC, Hynix etc to pay fair prices for wafers, has meant that there hasn't been any profit margin to fund thst transition, so at this point, wafer manufacturers full transition to 300mm, is today in 2021, at least 5 years behind meeting the industry's 2015 goals. Just to illustrate how much this shift would mean for supply: A Zen 3 CCD die measures 11.72x7.43mm. Roughly 300 fit on a 200mm wafer. With a 300mm wafer, that grows to over 700. We're talking roughly 2.5x the surface area and dies, "just" from this switch to a moderately bigger wafer. And considering how the various steps from blank start to cut, tested and dioxide processed dies scale in regards to time, we're talking an even higher increase in actual unit output. So in very many regards, the current silicon shortage experienced, that's gonna last for years to come, come down to fab operator's greed.

This is the sad reality of many large industries of massive profits. Their decades of strangleholds on essential material and component suppliers, already are or will soon come back to bite us in the arse. And the ones bearing the brunt of that, are the end customers. 


Newer gens of CPUs, APUs and GPUs where more producers and designs go with smaller chiplets solutions, will help (due to the yield improvements), so will cheaper/better scaling interposer solutions. But as things stand now, most operational fabs are running flat out, but demand for big complex fab silicon is so high from every corner of every related industry that everyone and their dog is still suffering big shortages.

text:
They are called Axial fans because the air move parallel to the axle, radial fans the fan moves radially from the axle that would be your blower style fan. Same terminology is used for axial and radial compressors found in for example gas turbines that you find in your jet or more commonly turbofan engine in an airliner. Old gas turbines often had radial compressors, single stage because radial fans/compressor can have a high static pressure but the flow is limited, but on the other hand you cant have flow of a fluid/gas if you cant overcome the resistant. Thats why radial fans are used on blower cards due to the tightly packed fin stack and not axial fans because they just cant maintain airflow due to poor airflow to pressure ration and that goes up exponentially with the diameter of a radial fan, only goes up with thickens of a axial fan but even that has limited returns on static pressure. The airflow vs pressure us called your Fan curve or "pump curve"m google "fan curve" or "pump curve" to see diagrams of that.
Also you invested in Delta fans, I have a few of those but one of mine has "stators", basically fixed fan blades behind the fan.
Those are common on Delta 80, 120mm fans and if you want to increase the static pressure on an axial fan or compressor you need stators, stators are the blades that gives you an increase in static pressure.
You can see this in gas turbines, like your turbofan on an airliner, they with have alternating compressor blades and stators, every time the working gas goes trough a stator you get a pressure increase.
So if you want to stack or run some sort of push/pull configuration in computer, like a rack server with stacked axial fans, they often use axial fans with stators on the DC motor hub because just staking axial fans with no stator is inefficient and wont net you the static pressure gains you want.

EVGA 680 gtx classified is a perfect example of a good blower style cooler exploiting the benefits of radial fans and there exponential gains in static pressure with increased diameter.
The card is about 1" longer and wider so much bigger vapor chamber based fin-stack, bigger radial fan so much better pressure at any give airflow, that combined with the now less restrictive heat sink gives you a much better airflow at a lower rpm and therefor lower noise level.
It was one of the best Blower style cooler made for its time,  It could match the best open-aircoolers in an openair test bench, it would outperform any opainrcooler in a closed case due to the fact that it dose not need help by case fans or gigantic holes in the case to get axes to cool air and also letting noise out from fans inside the case. All it needed was enough of an opening to suck all that air it needs in. That made it possible to build a sound proofed cool running system with a overclocked card with temps like an openair cooled card in an openbench environment.
set it down to msrp and buy it. dont spen more than $350

text: ​ Prophet Mufasa  Well, by running properly we mean performing properly, aren't we? That's where my point about performance came from. And while some games do perform better with more memory, others don't despite allocating it. The mere fact that a game allocates memory doesn't prove that it takes advantage from it. Saying 8GB is a necessity for gaming, even for high settings 1440p, is unsubstiantied - there's no data to support it. It just happens that cards capable of 1440p usually have 8GB. That said if you for example look up RTX 2060 (6GB) vs 2060 Super (8GB) comparisons, you'll see that the difference in performance is usually the same within a game regardless of resolution - about 6% and up to 10% in very few cases (one that I found). So even if we attribute the jump from 6% to 10% to less VRAM (and that's a big if in the first place), it means that you lose about 3-4% of performance, arguably a negligible loss, with less VRAM, and that's in a very small minority of games, and only if you run them at 4K, running exactly the same with all the others. Thus it's hard to say 8GB is necessary for gaming at the moment. It's a marketing gimmick.
